scope.start: 17b: Ravina's question to Rava about a get written and held back in the husband's pocket (the exchange begun at the end of 17b continues into 18a)
scope.end: 18b: the case of ten signatories brought before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, whose ruling opens on 19a

sections.title: Two More Challenges to the Zman Takanah
sections.gist: Ravina presses the dated-get ordinance with two more hard cases: a get held back after writing, and a get delivered from overseas many months after it was written.

children.title: The Pocket Get: Written but Withheld
children.gist: Ravina asks what happens when a husband writes a get, holds it back hoping for reconciliation, and later delivers it with its now-inaccurate date.

bullets.text: Ravina asks Rava: if a husband writes a get, puts it in his pocket hoping his wife will appease him, and later gives it to her anyway, does the outdated date invalidate the document?

Rava answers: a person does not hasten his own misfortune (*lo martia inish puranuta lenafshei*); one only writes a get once truly resolved to divorce, so the Sages did not need to legislate against this unlikely scenario.

children.title: Gittin from Overseas: A Months-Long Gap
children.gist: Ravina asks Rav Ashi how the takanah helps when an overseas get is written many months before it is actually delivered.

bullets.text: Ravina asks Rav Ashi: a get from overseas may be written in Nisan but not reach the wife until Tishrei — what does the dated-get takanah accomplish across such a long gap?

Rav Ashi answers: it is publicly known that such gittin do not take effect as of their written date; so if a dispute arises over produce sold in the interim, the wife must bring proof of when she actually received the get.
The community's awareness of the overseas gap itself is the safeguard: no one can be misled into treating the written date as the effective date.

sections.title: When Does the Three-Month Waiting Period Begin?
sections.gist: A divorced or widowed woman must wait three months before remarrying, and Rav and Shmuel debate whether that count starts from the get's writing or its delivery.

illustration.caption: The three-month wait, counted from ketivah by Shmuel and from netinah by Rav; the halacha follows Shmuel's count from the writing.

children.title: Rav and Shmuel Disagree: Netinah or Ketivah
children.gist: The Sages required the three-month wait to avoid doubts about a subsequent child's paternity, and Rav and Shmuel dispute when the count begins.

bullets.text: The Sages decreed that a divorced or widowed woman may not remarry within three months, to prevent uncertainty about a subsequent child's paternity.
Rav: the three months are counted from *netinah*, the delivery of the get.
Shmuel: the three months are counted from *ketivah*, the writing of the get.

children.title: Objection: Two Wives With Different Dates
children.gist: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya challenges Shmuel's position with a case of two wives who receive their gittin simultaneously but whose documents bear different dates.

bullets.text: Rav Natan bar Hoshaya objects to Shmuel: if two women in the same courtyard receive their gittin at the same moment, but one get was written long before delivery and the other closer to it, counting from ketivah would let one remarry before the other despite equal delivery — an implausible outcome.
Abaye answers that this is no difficulty: the date written on each woman's own get itself shows observers when she may remarry, so there is no confusion between the two cases.

children.title: Baraita Supporting Rav (Netinah)
children.gist: A baraita about an agent delayed on the road with a get supports counting the three months from delivery.

bullets.text: A baraita: if an agent carrying a get is delayed three months on the road, the wife must still wait a full three months from when the get actually reaches her hand — supporting Rav's position that the count starts at delivery.
The baraita adds that there is no concern of an "old get" (*get yashan*) here, since the husband was not secluded with her during the delay.

children.title: Baraita Supporting Shmuel (Ketivah)
children.gist: A baraita about a get deliberately withheld for three months supports counting the three months from writing.

bullets.text: A baraita: if a husband deposits a get with a trustee instructing him to withhold delivery for three months, once the trustee delivers it the wife may remarry immediately, since the three months already elapsed from the writing — supporting Shmuel.
Here too the baraita notes there is no concern of *get yashan*, since the husband evidently was not secluded with her once he dispatched the get.

children.title: Final Ruling: From the Time of Writing
children.gist: Later authorities split in practice, and the Gemara rules that the count follows the time of writing.

bullets.text: Rav Kahana, Rav Pappi and Rav Ashi counted in practice from the time of writing; Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua counted from the time of delivery.
The Gemara concludes: the halacha follows the time of writing.

sections.gist: The Gemara asks whether an unpaid ketubah, once it becomes collectible, loses its protected status and is cancelled like an ordinary loan at the close of the Sabbatical year.

children.title: Ketubah as a Tnai Beit Din
children.gist: Ordinary loans are cancelled by shemittah, but a ketubah, being a rabbinic condition of marriage rather than a private loan, is normally exempt — until it becomes collectible.

bullets.text: Shemittah cancels outstanding, collectable debts, but obligations classified as *tnai beit din* — rabbinic enactments rather than private loans — are exempt; the ketubah, instituted by the Sages as a condition of marriage, is such an obligation.
The question: once a ketubah becomes collectible, through divorce or the husband's death, but remains unpaid, does it shed its protected status and become subject to shemittah like an ordinary debt?

children.title: Rav: Both Pegimah and Zekifah Required
children.gist: Rav holds the ketubah is exposed to shemittah only once the woman has both collected partial payment and formally declared the remainder a loan.

bullets.text: Rav: the ketubah becomes cancellable by shemittah only once the woman has collected partial payment (*pegimah*) and established the remaining balance as a court-recognized loan (*zekifah*) — both conditions together.
A supporting baraita states this explicitly: if she performed pegimah without zekifah, or zekifah without pegimah, the ketubah is not cancelled until both have occurred.

children.title: Shmuel: Either Condition Alone Suffices
children.gist: Shmuel holds that partial collection or a formal declaration of loan, on its own, is enough to expose the ketubah to cancellation.

bullets.text: Shmuel: either collecting partial payment without declaring a loan, or declaring the whole amount a loan without having collected anything, suffices to expose the ketubah to shemittah.

A baraita lists other women's obligations — the fine for rape, for a false claim of non-virginity, and for seduction, along with the ketubah — as cancelled by shemittah once established as a loan (*zekifah*), defined as from when the matter stood judgment in court; it says nothing of pegimah.
The baraita only partly supports Shmuel: it shows zekifah alone can suffice, but is silent on whether pegimah alone, without zekifah, would also suffice.
Unlike the other disputes on this daf, the Gemara reaches no final ruling between Rav and Shmuel here.

sections.title: A Ketubah Written by Day, Signed by Night
sections.gist: Shmuel compares a ketubah to a court document that may be written and signed at different times, though the Gemara qualifies the proof brought for this from Rav's silence.

bullets.text: Shmuel: a ketubah is comparable to a court-issued document (*ma'aseh beit din*); just as such documents may be written by day and signed at night without being invalidated, so too a ketubah.
Case in point: R. Chiya bar Rav's ketubah was written on one day and signed on another, and Rav, who was present, raised no objection — suggesting he agrees with Shmuel.

The Gemara qualifies this: Rav's silence proves nothing, since the scribe and witnesses remained continuously engaged in that same matter (*oskim b'oto inyan*) from the day's writing until the night's signing.

A baraita from the school of R. Elazar b'R. Tzadok confirms: writing by day and signing at night invalidates a document only when the parties are not continuously engaged in the same matter; if they remain so engaged, it is valid.

children.title: Rava's Rationale: Once Resolved, No More Reconciliation
children.gist: Rava explains that Rabbi Shimon's leniency rests on the husband's irrevocable resolve, dated from the moment of writing.

bullets.text: The Gemara returns to the Mishnah's ruling that Rabbi Shimon validates a get written by day and signed at night.

Rava: Rabbi Shimon holds that once a husband has resolved to divorce — evident from the act of writing — he can no longer be reconciled (*ein lo piyus*); the wife's rights to the produce begin from that moment, regardless of when the get is later signed.

children.title: Reish Lakish Limits the Leniency to the Same Night
children.gist: Reish Lakish restricts Rabbi Shimon's ruling to a signing that follows immediately, rejecting a ten-day gap out of concern for reconciliation.

bullets.text: Reish Lakish: Rabbi Shimon validates the get only when signing follows immediately, the same night after writing; if the gap extends to ten days, Rabbi Shimon does not validate it.
The concern: over a longer gap the husband may have reconciled with and had relations with his wife, which would invalidate the get as an "old get" (*get yashan*).

children.title: R. Yochanan Extends the Leniency to Ten Days
children.gist: R. Yochanan permits even a ten-day gap under Rabbi Shimon's ruling, since a real reconciliation would become publicly known.

bullets.text: R. Yochanan: even a gap of up to ten days between writing and signing is valid according to Rabbi Shimon, because a genuine reconciliation would inevitably become publicly known — there is no need to suspect one occurred silently.

children.title: The Two Views: Two Witnesses or All Ten?
children.gist: The dispute concerns a husband who explicitly told all ten men to participate; R. Yochanan makes two of them witnesses and the rest a condition, while Reish Lakish makes all ten witnesses.

bullets.text: Case: a husband tells ten men, "Write a get for my wife" — since a get requires only two witnesses, what role do the other eight play?
A baraita (from the Mishnah on 66b) establishes that without the word *kulchem* ("all of you"), one person writes and two sign; the other eight need not be involved at all.
So the dispute must concern a case where the husband said *kulchem*, obligating all ten to participate in some way.
R. Yochanan: two of the ten sign as the halachic witnesses (*edim*); the rest sign only to satisfy the husband's condition (*tnai*) that all ten take part.
Reish Lakish: all ten function as full witnesses.

children.title: Practical Differences Between the Two Views
children.gist: The two positions diverge on whether the eight extra signers may sign later and whether a disqualified person among them invalidates the get.

bullets.text: If two of the ten sign on the day of writing and the rest sign only up to ten days later: R. Yochanan validates the get, since a condition (*tnai*) has no fixed time and can be fulfilled whenever; Reish Lakish invalidates it, since all witnesses must sign together.

If one of the ten is found to be a relative or otherwise disqualified: R. Yochanan validates the get, since the disqualified person was never a witness, only fulfilling the condition, and two valid witnesses remain; Reish Lakish invalidates it, since all ten were meant to be witnesses.

A further question, on R. Yochanan's view: if the disqualified person signed first, before the two valid witnesses — some say the get remains valid, since the husband never designated which two are the witnesses, so any two valid signatories suffice regardless of order; others say it is invalid, lest people mistakenly rely on a disqualified person's signature in ordinary documents. Both views are left standing.

rows: Sign only to satisfy the husband's stipulation (tnai)
Valid — a tnai has no fixed time
Valid — only the two witnesses must be fit
Invalid — all witnesses must sign together

sections.title: The Case Before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi
sections.gist: An actual case matching the ten-signatory dispute — two signed immediately, the rest up to ten days later — comes before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, whose ruling opens on the next daf.

bullets.text: A husband told ten men to write a get for his wife; two signed that day, and the rest signed only after a gap of up to ten days.
The case was brought before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi, who began to answer.

sections.continues: Continues on 19a: Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi rules that Rabbi Shimon's leniency may be relied on in exigent circumstances, and the Gemara works out that his ruling combines Rabbi Yochanan's ten-day extension of Rabbi Shimon's leniency with Reish Lakish's view that all ten signers are witnesses.

judgment_calls: Scope begins at 17b.13 (mid-exchange) rather than further back at Abaye's earlier questions to Rav Yosef on 17b, since those resolve entirely on 17b and only the final Ravina exchange spills onto 18a.

'A Ketubah Written by Day, Signed by Night' is kept as its own flat top-level section rather than nested under the shemittah discussion, since it addresses a distinct question (day/night signing) even though both concern ketubot.

The sub-dispute about a disqualified signer signing first (18b.6) is kept as a fine point inside 'Practical Differences' rather than split into its own section, since it only refines R. Yochanan's view already stated there.

'The Case Before Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi' is kept as a separate top-level section rather than a child of the ten-signatories discussion, since it is a new concrete case whose ruling spills onto the next daf.
coverage_notes: The shiur's review of the Yochanan/Reish Lakish debate on the purpose of zman (peirot vs. bas achoto) and Abaye's baraita of three invalid gittin not producing mamzerim belong to the previous daf (17b) and precede this daf's scope; not outlined here.
The essay names the amora presiding over the ten-day-gap case 'Rabbi Shimon ben Levi,' but the text names him 'Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi.' Followed the text.

The essay lists 'Rav Kahana, Rav Pappa, and Rav Ashi' for the ketivah ruling, but the text has 'Rav Kahana, Rav Pappi, and Rav Ashi' for ketivah and 'Rav Pappa and Rav Huna son of Rav Yehoshua' for netinah. Followed the text.
The shiur's discussion of Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi's full ruling (sha'at hadeichak, combining Yochanan and Reish Lakish) is drawn from 19a, outside this daf's text; noted only in the continues field.
